title: Like ...: Feelings and Situations
why: Native speakers often describe a feeling or a situation by pointing to a vivid little scene: a deer frozen in the headlights, a bull loose among the teacups. These similes let you say a lot about mood and behaviour in very few words.
know: eight similes for feelings and situations
able: describe your own reactions vividly: delight, panic, relief, restlessness
complain diplomatically about someone who won't listen or keeps repeating themselves
recognise when a simile has been shortened into a metaphor or a compound adjective
mistakes: He just stood there like a deer in the lights.
Like a deer in the headlights. The full noun is fixed; British speakers also say like a rabbit in the headlights.
My manager repeats himself like a broken disc.
Like a broken record. A literal translation (French disque rayé, Spanish disco rayado) doesn't work in English.
Criticism is like water on a duck's back to her.
Like water off a duck's back. The water runs off; the preposition is fixed.
He walked into the meeting as a bull in a china shop.
Like a bull in a china shop. As a bull would mean he really is a bull, in that role.
I was like a kid in a candy store, like a cat on a hot tin roof and like a deer in the headlights.
Pick one simile. Stacking clichés sounds comic or careless, not vivid.
bigidea: The as ... as similes compare one quality (as cold as ice). The like similes in this lesson compare a whole scene: a person, an animal or a situation that everyone can picture. When you say a new manager is like a bull in a china shop, the listener sees the bull, the fragile plates and the damage, all at once.

These similes usually follow verbs of perception and behaviour: feel like, look like, sound like, act like, or the frame it's like + a situation (it's like talking to a brick wall). They are mostly casual or humorous, so they suit conversation, emails to colleagues you know, and storytelling more than formal reports.

Many of them can lose the word like and become metaphors: she's a bull in a china shop, that's a red rag to a bull, a deer-in-the-headlights look. Keeping like sounds slightly softer; dropping it sounds more confident and more judgmental. One trap: the casual quotative she was like, "No way!" is not a simile at all.
hidden: After the hike I slept like a log.
The news spread like wildfire on social media.
Her new novel is selling like hot cakes.
A bit of vinegar on the stain worked like a charm.
My teenage son eats like a horse.

expressions.e: like a kid in a candy store
expressions.meaning: delighted and excited, especially by having lots of things to choose from
expressions.example: Give my dad an afternoon in a hardware store and he's like a kid in a candy store.
expressions.bend: Usually after be or feel: I felt like a kid in a candy store. British version: like a child in a sweet shop.
expressions.note: Region: candy store is North American, sweet shop British. Almost always used about adults, which is why it's funny. Can also hint at a lack of self-control.

expressions.e: like a deer in the headlights

pic.label: a deer and a car's headlights

expressions.meaning: frozen with shock or fear, unable to think or act
expressions.example: When the reporter asked about the missing funds, the spokesperson looked like a deer in the headlights.
expressions.bend: Also like a deer caught in the headlights, and as a compound adjective: a deer-in-the-headlights look.
expressions.note: Mainly North American. British speakers more often say like a rabbit in the headlights. Not the same as nervous: the key idea is freezing.

expressions.e: like a bull in a china shop

pic.label: a bull and china (teapots, cups and plates)

expressions.meaning: clumsy or tactless in a situation that needs care
expressions.example: He handled the merger talks like a bull in a china shop and offended both families.
expressions.bend: Often after act, behave, go in; also as a metaphor: he's a bull in a china shop.
expressions.note: China here means porcelain dishes, so lower case. It can describe physical clumsiness or, more often at C1 level, social and diplomatic clumsiness.

expressions.e: like talking to a brick wall
expressions.meaning: the other person doesn't listen or respond at all
expressions.example: I've asked the landlord about the heating five times. It's like talking to a brick wall.
expressions.bend: Usually it's like talking to a brick wall; also I might as well be talking to a brick wall.
expressions.note: Don't confuse with like banging your head against a brick wall, which means making a frustrating effort that achieves nothing.

expressions.e: like water off a duck's back
expressions.meaning: criticism or insults have no effect on someone
expressions.example: The coach yells a lot, but it's like water off a duck's back to the veterans.
expressions.bend: Often it's (just) like water off a duck's back (to him). Sometimes shortened: water off a duck's back.
expressions.note: Can be admiring (she's resilient) or critical (he never learns). Ducks' feathers are oily, so water runs off: the preposition is off.

expressions.e: like a red rag to a bull

pic.label: a bull and a red rag

expressions.meaning: certain to make a particular person very angry
expressions.example: Mentioning the parking fines at the council meeting was like a red rag to a bull.
expressions.bend: Often without like: it's a red rag to a bull. North Americans tend to say like waving a red flag in front of a bull.
expressions.note: Mainly British. Fun fact: bulls don't react to the colour red; it's the movement of the cape. The idiom doesn't care.

pic.label: a record (a disc that plays music)

expressions.meaning: saying the same thing again and again, annoyingly
expressions.example: I know I sound like a broken record, but please save your work before you leave.
expressions.bend: Usually sound like a broken record. British speakers also say like a stuck record.
expressions.note: From vinyl records that skip and repeat. Very common as a polite self-aware apology before repeating a reminder.

expressions.e: like a cat on a hot tin roof
expressions.meaning: nervous, restless and unable to keep still
expressions.example: Waiting for the biopsy results, she was like a cat on a hot tin roof all week.
expressions.bend: Usually after be; British speakers also say like a cat on hot bricks, the older form.
expressions.note: Made famous by Tennessee Williams's 1955 play title. Not the same as a deer in the headlights: the cat can't stop moving; the deer can't move.

culture.work: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof
culture.how: In this Pulitzer Prize-winning play set on a Mississippi plantation, Maggie describes her own state with the title image: anxious, unwanted by her husband Brick, but refusing to jump off. The simile captures a feeling of nervous endurance rather than panic.
culture.ask: When have you felt like a cat on a hot tin roof but decided to stay where you were?
culture.find: Tennessee Williams Cat on a Hot Tin Roof Maggie meaning of title

culture.how: Catherine explains her two loves to the housekeeper Nelly with two similes. Her love for the gentle Edgar Linton is like the leaves in a wood, which time will change; her love for Heathcliff is like the permanent rock underneath, not pleasant, but necessary. The contrast says more than any adjective could.
culture.ask: Catherine compares love to leaves and to rock. What would you compare a lasting friendship to?
culture.find: Wuthering Heights Catherine love foliage rocks speech chapter 9

culture.how: In the balcony scene, Romeo calls Juliet the sun: that's a metaphor, she is the sun. Juliet, more cautious, uses a simile: she says her love is as deep and limitless as the sea, and the more she gives, the more she has. Compare how bold the metaphor feels next to the simile.
culture.ask: Which sounds more convincing to you, the metaphor or the simile? Why?
culture.find: Romeo and Juliet balcony scene Juliet bounty as boundless as the sea

culture.how: The Montreal-born songwriter wrote it on the Greek island of Hydra. He compares himself to a bird perched on a wire and to other unsettled figures, and confesses that he has tried, in his own way, to be free. The song works as both an apology and a self-portrait.
culture.ask: What image would you choose to describe yourself at a restless time in your life?
culture.find: Leonard Cohen Bird on the Wire

like a kid in a candy store

like water off a duck's back

pick.q: Don't mention the referee to my brother. After last night's game, it's ___.

like night and day

opts: like a deer in the headlights
like a broken record
like a dog with a bone

spot.q: In the interview she looked like a deer in the lights when they asked about her gap year.
opts: a deer in the headlights
a deer in the spotlight
spot.why: The fixed phrase is like a deer in the headlights: frozen with shock.

spot.q: His insults are like water on a duck's back to me now.
opts: water off a duck's back
water under the bridge
spot.why: The water runs off the duck: like water off a duck's back.

spot.q: My father is like a broken disc about turning off the lights.
opts: a broken record
a broken clock
spot.why: English uses record, not disc: like a broken record.

spot.q: The intern charged into the client meeting like a cow in a china shop.
spot.bad: a cow in a china shop

opts: a bull in a china shop
a bull in a glass house
spot.why: The animal is fixed: like a bull in a china shop.

spot.q: Asking him for a straight answer is like talking to a stone wall.
opts: talking to a brick wall
talking to a closed door
spot.why: The usual noun is brick: it's like talking to a brick wall.

type.q: At the antiques fair, my partner was like a kid in a candy ___.
type.why: Like a kid in a candy store (North American). British: like a child in a sweet shop.

type.q: The minister froze like a deer in the ___ when the microphone was switched on.
type.why: Like a deer in the headlights: frozen with shock.

type.q: He's lovely, but in a negotiation he's like a bull in a china ___.
type.why: Like a bull in a china shop: clumsy where care is needed.

type.q: Telling my teenager to tidy his room is like talking to a brick ___.
type.why: Like talking to a brick wall: no one is listening.

type.q: Any mention of tax increases is like a red rag to a ___ for him.
type.why: Like a red rag to a bull: sure to provoke anger. Mainly British.

type.q: Waiting for the adoption call, they were like a cat on a hot tin ___.
type.why: Like a cat on a hot tin roof: nervous and restless. Older British form: on hot bricks.

bend.q: A team leader apologises before repeating a safety rule. Which version sounds natural? ___
opts: I know I sound like a broken record, but wear your helmets.
I know I sound as a broken record, but wear your helmets.
I know I sound like a broken disc, but wear your helmets.
bend.why: Sound like + noun phrase. As + noun would mean being a record; disc is a translation error.

bend.q: A British colleague drops the word like. Which version sounds natural? ___
opts: Late invoices are a red rag at a bull for her.
Late invoices are a red rag to a bull for her.
Late invoices are red rags to bulls for her.
bend.why: Like is often dropped: it's a red rag to a bull. The preposition to and the singular are fixed.

bend.q: A political commentator turns the simile into an adjective. Which version sounds natural? ___
opts: The candidate had a deer-of-the-headlights look.
The candidate had a headlights-deer look.
The candidate had a deer-in-the-headlights look.
bend.why: The whole phrase becomes a hyphenated adjective: a deer-in-the-headlights look.

bend.q: Someone adds an intensifier while telling a story about a bookshop. Which version sounds natural? ___
opts: I was just like a kid in a candy store.
I was like just kid in candy store.
I was as just a kid in a candy store.
bend.why: Just or really can go before like; the articles stay: just like a kid in a candy store.

talk: In Wuthering Heights, Catherine compares one love to leaves and another to rock. Choose two people or places in your life and compare them with two contrasting similes.
Tell a story about a time you felt like a deer in the headlights and another time you felt like a cat on a hot tin roof. What was the difference?
Role-play: you are a manager. One team member keeps ignoring your instructions. Complain to a trusted colleague using at least three similes from this lesson, then decide what to do.
Is it a good thing when criticism is like water off a duck's back for someone? When is it a strength, and when is it a weakness?
Romeo uses a metaphor and Juliet uses a simile. Change three similes from this lesson into metaphors. Do they sound stronger, ruder, or just different?
